# Intraosseous access

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Anesthesiology > Intraosseous access*

[Original Article Link](/library/It0YU3)

---

## Summary

Intraosseous (IO) access is an alternative route for administering medications, fluids, and <u>blood products</u> when peripheral or <u>central venous access</u> is not readily available. A large bore needle is passed through the bone cortex into the <u>intramedullary</u> space. Fluids and medications delivered through the IO needle are rapidly absorbed in the <u>intramedullary</u> sinusoids and delivered centrally. IO access is indicated whenever resuscitation is delayed by unsuccessful or difficult <u>peripheral IV access</u>. It is especially useful in <u>cardiac arrest</u>, <u>shock</u>, <u>severe dehydration</u>, and extensive <u>burns</u>. Multiple anatomic sites can be used for IO placement, and decision will depend on factors such as patient age and accessibility of the site. The <u>proximal</u> <u>tibia</u> is the most commonly used site. <u>IO needle insertion</u> is most commonly achieved using a semiautomatic insertion system. IO access should not be established in a limb with a <u>fracture</u>, infection, burn, or chronic pathologic condition. Complications are rare but include <u>IO extravasation</u> and infection.
